answer.label: Not Henry David Thoreau — actually Zig Ziglar
answer.sourceLine: This is a signature line of motivational author ‘Zig’ Ziglar. Quote Investigator found the earliest form in Ziglar’s 1974 book Biscuits, Fleas, and Pump Handles (retitled See You at the Top in 1975), where he wrote “what you get by reaching your goals is not nearly so important as what you become by reaching them.” The smoother “achieving your goals” phrasing is a later restatement of Ziglar’s own idea. There is no evidence Henry David Thoreau ever wrote it.

source.excerpt: What you get by achieving your goals is not as important as what you become by achieving your goals.
trail: Quote Investigator located the earliest match in Zig Ziglar’s 1974 Biscuits, Fleas, and Pump Handles, later reissued as See You at the Top (1975).

QI notes Ziglar returned to the idea repeatedly, e.g. “what you get by reaching your objective is not as important as what you become by reaching that objective,” and in 2012 credited the line to himself in Inspiration from the Top.
Per QI, the Thoreau credit surfaced only in a 2011 online post and a Goethe credit in a 2005 self-help book — both unsupported.
source.excerptNote: The popular “achieving your goals” form is a polished restatement; Ziglar’s earliest documented wording used “reaching your goals… not nearly so important as what you become by reaching them.”

author.name: Zig Ziglar
author.heading: Zig Ziglar
author.bio: Hilary Hinton “Zig” Ziglar was an American salesman turned motivational speaker whose 1975 book See You at the Top became a self-improvement bestseller. His folksy, goal-focused aphorisms — this among them — circulated so widely that they were often re-credited to older, more literary names.

misattribution.heading: How Thoreau got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a modern motivational maxim that later got draped over famous 19th-century names to lend it gravitas. Quote Investigator untangled the chain.

items.why: According to Quote Investigator, the Thoreau attribution appears only in a 2011 online post — nearly 150 years after Thoreau’s death (1862) — with no basis in any of his writings.
QI notes a 2005 self-help book credited Goethe (d. 1832); like the Thoreau version, it has no substantive supporting evidence.

misattribution.truthLine: The originator is motivational author Zig Ziglar, whose 1970s books contain the earliest documented forms of the saying, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why it gets misattributed
lead: The saying is a compact statement of Ziglar’s core theme: goals matter less for the prizes they hand you than for the person you have to become to reach them. It reads like timeless wisdom, which is exactly why it drifts toward names like Thoreau and Goethe.

Ziglar himself smoothed the wording over the years — from “reaching your goals… not nearly so important” toward the tighter modern form — so no single ‘canonical’ sentence exists, which further loosens it from its true source.
context.pull: The prize isn’t the point; who you become chasing it is.
